chunks: What to monitor while charging a LiPo. The question: What should you monitor when charging a LiPo?
While a lithium battery charges, you watch four things: the voltage of each cell, the current, the temperature and the time. A healthy charge has a very predictable pattern.
If any reading steps outside that pattern, something is wrong, and the charge should stop. The monitoring is what makes charging safe.
Think of watching a pot on the stove. You keep an eye on the heat, the level, and a timer. When it behaves as expected, you leave it.
If it starts to boil over, or the timer goes off, you act. The charger does that automatically and never looks away.
The difference is that a pot warns you with noise and steam, while a battery fault can be silent until it is serious.
Normalized to their limits, the voltage rises to 1. 0 and then stays pinned, while the current stays at 1. 0 and then decays to the 0. 05 (C/20) termination line.
The monitoring logic detects exactly these events: V reaching the limit (transition), and I falling below the threshold (end).
Per-cell voltage: the voltage of each cell on its own, which must stay at or below 4. 20 volts ("LiPo cell voltage range and why").
Cell spread: the voltage difference between the highest and lowest cell in a pack ("Cell balancing: why, when, what if missing").
Charge current profile: flat during CC, then falling during CV ("Constant-current and constant-voltage charge phases").
NTC thermistor: the temperature sensor on the cell ("What to monitor in a LiPo circuit"). Safety timer: a time limit that ends charging even if nothing else stops it.
Charge a 2 Ah cell at 1C. A healthy charge looks like this. The current sits flat at 2 amps. The voltage climbs to 4. 2 volts and is held there.
The current then decays to about 0. 1 to 0. 2 amps, and the charger stops after roughly 77 minutes.
The cell warms only a few degrees, since 2 amps through 50 milliohms makes just 2 squared times 0. 05 equals 0. 2 watts.
A rise of about a degree per minute or more, or a current that will not taper, is a red flag. That is the whole idea.
"Per-cell voltage, current, temperature and time. Each cell must stay at or below 4. 2 volts and I watch the spread in a series pack.
Current should hold at the set value in CC, then taper in CV until about C over 20 to C over 10, where I terminate.
Temperature from an NTC, within about 0 to 45 degrees and without a fast rise. And a safety timer as a backstop. A healthy charge is flat current, voltage pinned at 4.
2, current decaying; a stuck current, a hot cell or a cell out of line means stop."
